properties.name: The batch write buffer gets an index; hydrate 8.83s → 0.91s
properties.rationale:
THE CAUSE WAS FOUND BY ARITHMETIC BEFORE IT WAS FOUND BY A PROFILER, and the arithmetic is why the diagnosis was trustworthy. Buffer at end of import ~44,000 ops; average during the edge loop ~23,000; two endpoint checks per edge gives 2 x 13,390 x 23,000 = ~616M comparisons. Divided into the measured 8,398 ms that is ~13.6 ns per comparison — exactly what a branch plus a slice compare costs. The model also predicted the 2,000-node point at 0.99 s against 1.14 s measured, so it was checked at two scales before any code changed.

⭐ THE FIRST HYPOTHESIS WAS WRONG AND SAYING SO IS THE LESSON. The obvious guess was "adjacency lists are read-modify-write per edge insert". Reading the code killed it: `adj_out_key(graph_id, from_id, edge_type, to_id)` includes the target id, so every edge is its OWN key — three puts, no reads. The real cost was on the READ side, in a helper nobody would look at when thinking about write performance. **A performance guess that names a plausible mechanism is worth exactly nothing until the code is read.**

⚠️ WHAT WAS DELIBERATELY NOT DONE: `import_graph` already builds a map of every node id in the document, so it could have skipped the endpoint existence check entirely and got a similar speedup. Rejected — that weakens a store invariant (`create_edge` refuses dangling edges, and the comment above it records the defect that motivated the refusal) to work around a lookup bug, and it would have fixed exactly one caller while leaving every other batch reader slow.

VERIFIED: 1,452 core tests pass, including the two corners this could have broken — `buffer_aware_get_late_put_resurrects_after_prefix_delete` and `batch_prefix_delete_visible_within_batch`. clippy `--all-targets -D warnings` and fmt clean. clippy also caught the now-dead `BufferedOp::affecting`, the linear-scan helper this replaced, which was removed.
properties.subject: system
properties.summary:
`StorageEngine`'s write buffer was a bare `Vec<BufferedOp>`, and every buffered read did `buffer.iter().rev().find_map(|op| op.affecting(cf, key))` — a linear scan of the entire buffer, per lookup. `DesignGraph::create_edge` checks that both endpoints exist, so importing a design costs two buffered reads per edge while the buffer keeps growing, which is quadratic.

The buffer is now a `WriteBuffer` struct: the ordered `Vec` is kept (the backend applies it in order, and a late Put must resurrect a key an earlier PrefixDelete tombstoned), with a `BTreeMap<(CfId, Vec<u8>), usize>` mapping an exact key to the POSITION of its latest Put/Delete, plus a separate small list of PrefixDelete positions. Lookups resolve by comparing positions, so ordering semantics are unchanged. `BTreeMap` rather than `HashMap` because the same index also serves `prefix_scan`, whose pre-flight (`buffer_touches_scan`, now deleted) was a second linear walk — it is answered by a range query now, and the overlay applies only the ops that actually bear on the range, still in insertion order.

MEASURED on reflow2's own design (3,140 nodes / 13,390 edges), release, in-memory backend, no full-text index:

    TOTAL to queryable   8,828 ms  ->    909 ms   (9.7x)
    of which import      8,398 ms  ->    705 ms  (11.9x)

Every batch reader benefits, not just import: the bulk tools, `apply_heal` and merge application all read through the same buffered path.
